meta.title: Keshavji Naik Chawl Ganpati
meta.location: Keshavji Naik Chawl, Khadilkar Road, Girgaon, Mumbai 400004
meta.foundedNote: 1893 is supported by the institution and BMC heritage account; priority claims are retained as attributed descriptions, not an all-India first.
meta.intro: A small Ganapati in a Girgaon chawl courtyard anchors a public festival traced to 1893. The Shree Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Sanstha preserves a tradition associated with Lokmanya Tilak while residents sustain worship, talks and cultural programmes. Its archive is unusually rich in printed invitations, schedules and newspaper cuttings. This collection follows that documentary trail alongside the More family's idol-making association, keeping the separate Nikadwari Lane Girgaoncha Raja institution distinct.

sections.title: A festival rooted in a courtyard

paragraphs.text: The festival dates to 1893 in both the institution's narrative and the municipal heritage account. The latter describes local organisers and an early move from a resident's apartment into the shared courtyard. This places household worship, public assembly and the architecture of the chawl within the same story.

Lokmanya Tilak's 1901 visit is a documented institutional landmark. Calling the celebration Tilak-inspired is better supported than collapsing every local founder into a claim that he personally organised it. The 1893 priority is a Mumbai historical claim; it is not treated here as proof of the first public Ganesh festival anywhere.

Rediff's retrospective associates the small courtyard idol with the More family. The current institutional account identifies Rajendra More as a later-generation maker and describes restraint in amplification and display. Exact height and the number of sculptor generations should be attached to dated evidence rather than assumed constant.

Surviving 1934 and 1946 programmes show that the festival archive extends beyond images of the deity. The 1946 sheet combines installation, games and devotional performance. In 2026, reporting described Warli-themed preparation and planned lectures, showing how cultural programming can change while the courtyard remains the organising setting.

sections.title: The small form, the makers and the work around it

paragraphs.text: Varsha Mahajan's Marathi anniversary recollection describes the festival through household labour: preparing ritual vessels, buying flowers, sharing food and gathering for recitation and performance. She recalls a stable seated form and the palanquin custom. Her account also dates constitutional approval to 1935 and a Tilak re-enactment to 2001. These are attributed resident memories, useful leads for the institution's surviving minutes and programmes rather than substitutes for them.

Mid-day's 2017 preparations report identifies Rajendra More in his Girgaum workshop and associates the commission with four generations of artisans. Its maker portrait is carefully distinguished from a verified photograph of the finished 2017 idol. The same report identifies the current Ganpatipule temple setting, allowing an annual decoration attribution without treating the article's sculpture foreground as the installed idol.

The 2021 pandemic account provides a specific continuity test: unlike mandals forced to reduce large idols, Keshavji already used a2.25 ft form, according to the report. Its organiser also described educational supplies sent to a Chiplun school. The archive records that year's reported policy and welfare work without inventing a 2021 image.

Clear idol views from the 2018 and 2024 Rediff visits extend the photographic record with Satish Bodas' credit. The 2024 palanquin scene also documents the carrying object and physical chawl environment. A separately identified 2025 agency preview adds a precisely captioned date, with publication permission still unknown. The 2023 two-frame press animation remains a dated publication object whose individual photographic years are unconfirmed.

media.label: Animated photograph sequence - capture year uncertain

media.credit: Srishti Kapoor / The Indian Express (the source credits the plural photographs).
media.dateEvidence: The GIF accompanies a specifically captioned Keshavji section in a report first published26 September 2023 and later updated7 September 2024. No individual frame explicitly states its capture year.2023 indexes the report object; neither frame is independently authenticated as a 2023 capture, and the later update does not prove 2024.

visualReview.observedForm: Both source GIF frames were viewed: one shows the institution-labelled entrance, white temporary temple columns, red carpet and distant Ganesh; the other shows a small four-armed seated Ganesh in yellow dhoti and purple cushion/backing on an elaborate silver arched throne, with flowers and offering vessels.
visualReview.note: Every frame, not only the first, was visually inspected. The two scenes have compatible physical stage/throne details; this does not establish their capture year. Original animated GIF retained unchanged.

researchNotes.coverage: Official history/gallery, BMC heritage account, Rediff retrospective and 2026 contemporary report; five dated media objects inspected. A clearly captioned 2022 Indian Express palanquin photograph supplies the idol hero; archive scans are documents. Phase 2: 6 annual entries supplemented after direct image inspection; source labels and photographic appearance assessed separately.
